title: A Clay Which Is As White
logline: A captive sailor finished his own house by whitening its walls with lime, and was told he had committed a capital offence: lime was for the king's houses and the temples. The people, he noted, had a clay that was just as white. The walls the rule kept for the king still stand white beside a lake, with a whole hillside of white houses around them now, and from any distance no one can say which white was the forbidden one.
human_question: If the thing I will not let anyone else have looks exactly like what they already have, what is it that I am keeping?

place.what_kind_of_place: The last royal precinct of the island's hill kingdom, at the head of an artificial lake in a basin of wooded hills: long white outer walls, a white octagonal pavilion raised on a stepped and moulded base under a red roof, royal residences, an open audience hall, and a lake-edge pavilion standing in the water. Along the lake's shore on the precinct side runs a low white parapet several hundred metres long, its top scalloped like a line of cloud and pierced with rows of small triangular openings. The hills that close the basin were once the kingdom's; they are now covered, slope above slope, with ordinary houses, most of them white or cream.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: It is one of the island's great set pieces: a white royal and temple front reflected in a lake, framed by forest and hills, seen from a viewpoint high on the opposite slope. With the sound off the film is a study of white under an even sky: a scalloped wall doubled in still water, a pale octagon on its tiers of mouldings, the grain and repairs of washed plaster at arm's length, and then a hillside of houses in which the same white appears a hundred times. Its one move, repeated, is a slow optical zoom out from a frame that is nothing but white, which keeps the viewer guessing what surface it is until the lens has pulled back far enough to say.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Almost nothing but the lens. Every shot is locked on a tripod and makes one continuous zoom from the long end to the wide end, never panning, never cutting inside the move; the only things that move within the frame are the water, the birds on it, and the cloud. The light is chosen not to change: high, even cloud with no sun, so that no white casts a shadow or catches a highlight that would tell one surface from another. No person is framed at any point.
place.when_it_looks_best: A still, overcast late morning outside the monsoon peaks, with high bright cloud rather than rain, when the lake lies flat enough to hold a reflection and the hills are clear of mist. Hard sun is wrong for this film: it separates the whites into glare and shade and makes the materials look different, which is exactly what the documents say they did not.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A white film. Each shot opens on a frame of pure, shadowless white and pulls slowly back until it becomes something: a cloud-shaped parapet on a lake, a tiered octagon, a plastered wall with its patches and streaks, an ordinary house on a hillside. The last shot starts on white and keeps pulling back from the top of a hill until a whole basin is in frame, a lake, a royal precinct and a town, every wall in it pale under the same grey sky. A viewer with no interest in philosophy gets a complete, calm piece about looking closely and then looking from far away.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same zooms become a question about a rule. A captive sailor's book of 1681 says that lime-white walls were reserved to royal houses and temples on pain of what he called a capital offence, and in the same book says that the people had a clay that was just as white. So the rule reserved a material the eye could not tell from its substitute. The voice sets that beside the texts' account of stinginess: born of attachment to one's own things, but showing itself as not bearing them to become common, and therefore counted with aversion, never with greed; with four marks, one of which is not bearing that another should have something like one's own, and five things it fastens on, the first of them a dwelling. Then it declines the easy verdict. The texts describe single moments of mind that come one at a time and go; a rule described across a hundred and forty years and seven reigns is not a moment, and no one's mind can be read off a wall. The film's own method is the admission: every zoom begins where the camera cannot tell what the white is, and the last one ends where it still cannot tell which white was forbidden.

sequence.on_screen: Late morning under high, even cloud. On a tripod on the lake's far bank, the lens at its longest: the frame is entirely white, flat, without a shadow or an edge. It holds for a few seconds, then a single slow zoom out begins, with no pan. Small dark triangles appear in the white, then a line of water beneath it, and the white becomes a long low parapet along the edge of a lake, its top scalloped like a row of clouds, doubled in the still water.
sequence.voice: In 1681 an English sailor named Robert Knox published an account of nearly twenty years held captive in this island's hill kingdom. In the first years of his captivity, he writes, the villagers built him a house. They were called away before it was finished, so he and his boy finished it themselves, and whitened the walls with lime, the way it was done at home.

sequence.on_screen: A second zoom out, again from pure white. The white separates into a cornice, then into tier after tier of plain white mouldings, and pulls back to an octagonal pavilion standing on a white base under a red roof, beside long white walls. Nobody in the frame.
sequence.voice: 'But in doing this,' he wrote, 'I committed a Capital Offence: for none may white their Houses with Lime, that being peculiar to Royal Houses and Temples.' A native who had done it, he thought, would most probably have paid with his head, or at the least a great fine. Nothing was done to him. He was a stranger, and he had done it in ignorance.

sequence.on_screen: Close and frontal in the flat light: a stretch of plastered wall in the precinct, framed so that no edge, window or moulding shows. Only texture: the grain of the wash, faint streaks where water has run, a patch of repair in a very slightly different white. A short zoom out stops while the frame is still nothing but wall.
sequence.voice: In another chapter he describes the people's houses: low, one storey, walls of daubed clay. They might not roof them with tiles, he says, 'nor whiten their walls with lime, but there is a Clay which is as white, and that they use sometimes.' A surgeon with the army that ended the kingdom wrote the same a hundred and forty years later: the chiefs washed their walls with white clay, the use of lime being prohibited. So the rule did not keep a colour. The clay was as white. It kept a material, and by the captive's account the eye would not have known the difference.

sequence.on_screen: From the slope opposite the precinct, a zoom out from another white: it resolves into the side of an ordinary house, then into its neighbours, cream and white walls stacked up a wooded hillside under red and grey roofs, dozens of them, none of them anyone's palace.
sequence.voice: The texts this series follows have a name for not bearing that what is one's own should become common to others. They call it stinginess, and they do something unexpected with it. It grows, they say, out of attachment to one's own things. And yet, because it shows itself as not bearing those things to be shared, it never arises with greed. It arises only with aversion.

sequence.on_screen: Back at the water's edge, low: a zoom out that begins on the white of the parapet's reflection in the lake, rippling slightly, until the wall itself comes into the top of the frame and the two whites, the stone and its image, run side by side away along the shore.
sequence.voice: The rule, as the captive wrote it down, has the same shape. It does not say that the king's house shall be white. It says that no one else's may be. The texts give stinginess four marks, and one of them is not bearing that anyone else should have something like one's own. They also list five things it fastens on. The first is a dwelling.

sequence.on_screen: From the far bank, a long zoom out from the precinct's white outer wall until the octagon, the long walls, the water pavilion and the parapet are all in frame across the lake, small and pale against the forest behind them. Held.
sequence.voice: But the texts describe moments of mind, not laws. Envy, stinginess and remorse, they say, arise only with aversion, only sometimes, and never together: one at a time, for a moment, and gone. This rule was described by the captive in 1681 and again by the surgeon after 1815, across the reigns of seven kings. Whatever it was, it was not a moment. The texts give no way to read a mind off a wall, and this film does not try to read anyone's: not the king who held the captive, not the kings who built these walls, not anyone who lived under them.

sequence.on_screen: The payoff. From the viewpoint high above the lake, the last zoom starts on a white that fills the frame and pulls back without stopping: a wall, a house, a row of houses, the slope, and at last the whole basin, the lake, the cloud-shaped parapet, the octagon and the long white walls on the far shore, and around them the town's hundreds of pale walls, all under the same flat sky. The zoom reaches its widest and holds. No voice for the last part of the hold.
sequence.voice: Every account of this rule this film could find was written by an outsider: the captive, the surgeon, and the officers and scholars who came after them. They do not even agree on its terms. One says the king could give leave; one lets the highest officers plaster their walls; the surgeon says even the chiefs used clay. None of them says when it ended. From up here the king's white and the white of anyone's house cannot be told apart. By the captive's own account, they never could.

concept_merge.why_together: C026 supplies the film's central and slightly strange fact about stinginess: Margaya says it springs from greed attached to one's own things, yet because it arises as not bearing one's own things to become common to others, it arises only with hate and never with greed [C026-M:L19]. It also supplies the limit the film has to respect: envy, stinginess and remorse arise only with hate, only on some occasions, and never together in one mind, each arising separately [C026-P:L39; C026-M:L7]. C022 supplies the detail that lets the documents meet the doctrine without forcing: Pradeepika's four marks of stinginess, which include not bearing that another should have wealth like one's own, its object being one's own things where envy's is another's, and its reach to preventing others' giving [C022-P:L133]; the five kinds named by what stinginess fastens on, of which the first is a dwelling [C022-P:L135; C022-M:L45]; and Margaya's parallel four aspects [C022-M:L43]. Together they let one rule be read against a definition without reading anyone's mind: C022 says what the texts call the not-bearing, and C026 says where it sits and how briefly.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That a sumptuary rule can be a nearly pure case of the definition, and that this makes it harder, not easier, to call it anyone's stinginess. Knox's own sentence removes the other obvious readings: the colour was not scarce and not reserved, because the people had 'a Clay which is as white'; what was reserved was only that the lime should not become common, which is very close to the Margaya's account of how stinginess shows itself [C026-M:L19]. And yet C026's rule that these factors come only sometimes and one at a time [C026-P:L39] means the texts would look for it in single moments, while the rule is described across a hundred and forty years and seven reigns. So the pairing shows the gap between a definition and a verdict. The film uses the definition on the documents' words and refuses the verdict on any person, which is also what the C026 digest demands when it says the scheme is not a formula for reading people and a camera cannot show which factor is present.

concept_links.why: C026 needs its most counter-intuitive finding to be seen: that stinginess, though it springs from attachment to one's own things, arises as not bearing those things to become common to others, and so sits with aversion and never with greed [C026-M:L19]. The digest's does_not_transfer forbids the common equation of stinginess with greed on exactly this line, and the film is built to honour it. Knox's rule is a documented prohibition whose whole content is that something must not become common: it grants nothing to its owner that a permitted clay did not already give, since that clay was 'as white'; it only forbids others the lime. The second C026 finding sets the film's limit: envy, stinginess and remorse arise only with hate, only occasionally, and never together, each on its own [C026-P:L39; C026-M:L7]. A rule attested from 1681 to after 1815 cannot be a moment of that kind, so the film places the definition beside the rule and declines to call the rule, or any king, stingy. The digest's caution that the scheme is not a psychological formula for reading people and that a camera cannot show which factor is present is kept literally: the film's method is a camera that cannot tell which white is which.

C022 supplies the anatomy the rule is read against. Pradeepika gives stinginess the mark of concealing one's own wealth and lists what it will not bear: another owning something of one's own, another benefiting from it, another having wealth like one's own, and others even knowing of it; it takes one's own things as its object, where envy takes another's, and it will prevent others' giving if it can [C022-P:L133]. Margaya gives the same four aspects, with one wording uncertain in the OCR [C022-M:L43]. Both name five kinds by what stinginess fastens on, the first being a dwelling [C022-P:L135; C022-M:L45]. The rule against lime is compared with the third of Pradeepika's marks, and the voice names the dwelling only as the first of the five words, without gloss. The digest's reading that stinginess and envy are both placed with anger, and are forms of displeasure rather than of enjoyment, keeps the film from treating a reserved white as a display of pride.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That the texts define stinginess not as wanting to keep but as not bearing that one's own should become common, which is why they count it with aversion rather than with greed; that a real rule once reserved lime-white walls to the king's houses and the temples although a clay just as white was allowed to everyone; that such a rule matches the definition closely and still cannot be called anyone's stinginess, because the texts describe single passing moments and nobody's mind can be read off a wall. The proof is on screen: every zoom starts where the camera cannot tell what the white is, and the last one ends where it still cannot tell which white was forbidden.
what_must_be_real: The walls as they are, in the light they are in. No white is brightened, tinted, matched or separated in the grade to make the royal surfaces look different from the houses, or to make them look the same; if they differ on the day, the film shows that and says so. The zooms are real single optical moves, never stitched from separate shots or faked with digital cropping. No worshipper, visitor, guard, resident or passer-by is framed: many people at the temple wear white, so no zoom may start on or pass through clothing, and every zoom starts on a wall above head height or at a distance where no one can be identified. No ritual, offering, relic or interior of the temple is filmed, and no ritual sound is used. The voice quotes Knox and describes the other writers as texts; no king, builder, chief or householder is narrated as stingy, envious, proud or afraid.
position_hint: In the anger-and-fear stage, after the films that introduce the hate-rooted minds, as the group's film on the factors that ride on aversion and come one at a time: the quietest of them, stinginess, shown in a rule rather than in a person.
risks: Calling the rule, or a king, stingy. The whole concept fit invites it, and the brief forbids it. The voice gives the definition, gives the rule, and then says in so many words that the texts describe moments, not laws, and that no mind is read off a wall.

Mind-reading by quotation. Later writers do read the kings' minds: one British officer says the rule was one of the 'arts' by which mean buildings passed for a splendid palace, and the surgeon's history, in the passage that dates the lake and the octagon, calls the last king a tyrant. None of this is quoted or paraphrased in the voice.

Taking half of Knox. Retellings keep 'Capital Offence' and drop the rest: that it was Knox's own supposition that a native 'most probably' would have lost his head 'or at the least' been fined, that nothing was done to him, and that the people had a clay as white. The film uses the whole passage or none of it.

Knox's colour passage. In the same book Knox says the people held white to be honoured and black 'rejected', and lists among white men's privileges that their houses 'may be whitened with Lime'. That passage is racial, and it cannot be used in any form, including as an irony about the white walls.

Caste. The rules around dress and building were bound up with rank and caste, and a later scholar's summary of them sits beside caste occupations; the lime-burners who supplied the king's store were a named community. The voice says only 'the people', 'the chiefs' and 'the highest officers', and names no caste or community.

A live religious site. The precinct includes the island's most important temple, which is in daily use and under security. It appears only as white outer walls and the octagon seen from outside and from across the water; no devotee, no ritual, no relic, no interior, and no question about the relic enters the film.
The lake's legends. Popular stories about the lake (a harem island, tunnels, executions on the lake bed) are attested only by conquerors or not at all; none is used.

Overlap with a proposed film in the same group that also turns on stinginess: a copied mansion and a refused set of plans, built on the rule that conceit and stinginess can never share a moment. This film does not use that rule; it is built on stinginess sitting with aversion and on the factors coming one at a time.

The threshold-stone failure in a new form: a film of white walls under a grey sky could be flat. It survives only if the zooms genuinely withhold what the white is and the last one opens onto the whole basin; if the day gives neither, the film should not be made from postcards.
drop_if: Permission cannot be had to film the precinct's white walls from the public shore and the opposite hill with a tripod and a long zoom, or the temple authorities object to the temple's walls being used in a film about a prohibition.
The precinct's surfaces are under scaffolding or wrapped for restoration during the shooting window, so that no zoom can start on a clean white.

On the ground the royal whites and the hillside's whites turn out to be so plainly different under cloud (in tone, in texture, in finish) that the payoff would say something the film cannot honestly say. The voice's closing claim about the captive's account would still be true, but the image would contradict the words, and the film would need a new payoff or should be dropped.

connections.note: Another object of the same hill kingdom, in another group: a gold-sheathed throne in a museum case, approached in seven kneeling-height stops at night, on three envoys who saw gilt, solid gold and plating. There the question is what the eye took the material to be; here the documents say the eye could not tell the reserved material from the permitted one. That film is interior, lamplit and on its knees; this one is exterior, under flat cloud, and never moves the camera, only the lens.

Proposed for the same group and the same concept pair: a mansion said to have been copied after a rival refused its plans, on the rule that conceit and stinginess never share a moment. Both films touch stinginess; this one leaves conceit out entirely and stands on two other findings, that stinginess arises with aversion though it springs from attachment, and that it comes only sometimes and one at a time. That film is an interior dolly through doors at dusk; this one is exterior, overcast, and built on the zoom.

The group's other film built on a king's rule in writing: a slab that urges its readers to remove a man for a thought. Both refuse to read a king's mind off his text. That film reads a stone at page height in first raking sun and travels; this one stands still under cloud and uses only the lens, and its document is an outsider's book, not the king's own words.

selection.reason: Carries C026's hardest finding, that stinginess springs from attachment but arises as not bearing one's own to become common and so sits with aversion, on a documented rule whose only content is exactly that: a material reserved although a permitted substitute looked the same. The location is a first-rate landmark where the reserved white still stands inside a basin of everyone's white. The blind proposal was tested and kept, with its central claim corrected (the rule reserved lime, not a colour) and its treatment replaced to avoid two films in the same group.

review.note: The body of this record was replaced entirely on 2026-09-26 in the blind GRP-03 rework and rebuilt from fresh research; the previous body was not read. Under standing decision 9 the verdict is pending; the old status was also pending, so no confirmation or rejection has been reset. The concepts are unchanged (C026 primary, C022 supporting). The title changed to follow the film, and the two earlier titles are kept as aliases. The location, named in suggested_location, is the white-walled royal and temple precinct at the head of an artificial lake in the old hill capital, with the scalloped lake parapet and the town's hillsides; it takes its district from 3 to 4 films, since no other GRP-02 or GRP-03 film is now proposed there. It was a blind colleague's proposal and was tested, not assumed. Both halves hold: a primary, eyewitness text (Knox, 1681) sets out a rule reserving lime-white to royal houses and temples, which is very close to Margaya's account of stinginess as not bearing one's own to become common; and the place is one of the island's great views. Corrections made to the proposal and its sources: the rule did not reserve a colour, as the proposal's 'a colour only the king could own' says, because Knox writes in the same sentence that the people had 'a Clay which is as white', and an 1821 account says the chiefs used white clay; the 'capital offence' is Knox's own supposition ('most probable ... or at the least a great Fine') about a native, and nothing was done to him; the 'with the king's permission' wording is Forbes's (1840, vol. I p. 78), not a vague later gloss; D'Oyly's Sketch, in its 1833 journal printing, was searched and contains no rule on lime, whitewash, tiles or storeys; and the proposal's treatment (hard noon, a locked 200 mm lens from the hills) was replaced because two finished films in this group already use a locked noon frame and a locked long lens. The new treatment is an overcast film built entirely of single optical zoom-outs from pure white, with no drone and no camera movement. The strongest objection is that a law is not a mind, so the doctrinal fit risks exactly the analogy the texts' own digest forbids; the film answers it by saying so in the voice and refusing any verdict on any person. Still unverified: whether today's white on the royal buildings is lime at all, when the rule ended, permissions for tripod work on the shore and the viewpoint, and whether the whites really read alike on camera under cloud.

suggested_location.name: The royal palace and temple precinct of Kandy at the head of Kandy Lake: the white outer walls of the Sri Dalada Maligawa (Temple of the Sacred Tooth Relic) and the octagonal Pattirippuwa, the palace buildings beside them, the Walakulu Bemma (the 'cloud wall' parapet) along the lake, and the hillsides of the town seen from the Arthur's Seat viewpoint on Rajapihilla Mawatha

also_known_as.name: Kiri Muhuda
also_known_as.used_by: Sinhala usage, as reported on Wikipedia

suggested_location.region: Kandy District, Central Province: the precinct stands on the north shore of Kandy Lake in the centre of Kandy town, within the UNESCO World Heritage property of the Sacred City of Kandy; the Arthur's Seat viewpoint is on Rajapihilla Mawatha on the slope south-west of the lake, also in Kandy District
suggested_location.why_here: Because this is where the lime-white the rule reserved still stands, and the only place where it can be framed together with the white that everyone now has. Knox's rule, confirmed by an 1821 eyewitness, reserved lime-white to 'Royal Houses and Temples' and forbade it to everyone else although a clay 'as white' was allowed; the buildings of the kingdom's last royal precinct, including an octagon and a lake parapet built in its final reign, were raised under that rule. C026's hardest finding is that stinginess, though it springs from attachment, shows itself as not bearing one's own to become common, and so belongs with aversion: a rule whose only effect was that a material not become common, when its look was already common, is as near as a document comes to that definition. And the place is worth travelling for: a white royal and temple front on a lake in a basin of forest and hills, with one of the island's classic viewpoints above it, and hillsides that are now white with ordinary houses. It also carries the film's honest limit: nobody looking at it can tell which white was forbidden.

historical_thread.story:
Robert Knox, an English East India Company sailor, was taken with his father and others on the east coast in 1660 and held in the hill kingdom until he escaped in 1679. His book, An Historical Relation of the Island Ceylon (London, 1681, printed by the Royal Society's printer), describes the rule twice. In Part III, chapter VI, on the people's houses: 'Their Houses are small, low, thatched Cottages, built with sticks, daubed with clay, the walls made very smooth. For they are not permitted to build their houses above one story high, neither may they cover with tiles, nor whiten their walls with lime, but there is a Clay which is as white, and that they use sometimes ... Neither doth the King allow them to build better.' In Part IV, chapter III, on his own life, after villagers began a house for him in a garden of the king's coconut trees and he and his boy finished it: '[I] whitened the Walls with Lime, according to my own Countrey fashion. But in doing this I committed a Capital Offence: for none may white their Houses with Lime, that being peculiar to Royal Houses and Temples. But being a Stranger nothing was made of it, because I did it in ignorance: had it been a Native that had so done, it is most probable it would have cost him his Head, or at the least a great Fine.' Knox also records, in Part II, chapter I, that the king had stone pedestals 'whitened with Lime and laid in Oyl, so that they look purely white', on which he stood 'that he might be above the rest of the People'; and, in Part IV, chapter XIV, that white men were allowed, among other privileges, houses that 'may be whitened with Lime'.

A hundred and forty years later John Davy, surgeon to the British forces after the annexation of 1815, wrote in An Account of the Interior of Ceylon (1821), p. 256, that the chiefs' houses were 'of mud with tiled roofs ... always of a single story', their walls covered 'with a wash of white clay, the use of lime for the purpose being prohibited, and appropriated solely to royal palaces and temples', and that the dwellings of the people 'are invariably thatched; only those of the highest rank being permitted to have tiled roofs'. In his history (p. 317) he lists among the last king's public works 'the lake of Kandy, which was made at this time' and 'many new buildings, particularly the present Pattiripooa', in a passage set after about 1806. Jonathan Forbes, a British officer in the former kingdom's provinces, wrote in Eleven Years in Ceylon (1840), vol. I p. 78, that the king 'did not permit any person to have a house two stories high, nor to build one with windows, nor even to roof with tiles, nor whitewash mud walls, without obtaining the royal sanction', and read it as one of the 'arts' by which 'the mean buildings of the royal residence' seemed splendid. Ananda Coomaraswamy, in Mediaeval Sinhalese Art (1908), pp. 33–34, summarised the 'well-defined sumptuary laws': 'plastered walls, tiled roofs, finials and two-storied buildings were forbidden to all save the King, temples, and the highest officers'; at p. 135 he quotes Forbes and Davy and adds that only the king's palace and religious buildings might 'be plastered with lime'.

Who wrote it down, and what did they stand to gain. Every account reached is an outsider's. Knox wrote as an escaped captive whose book, printed by the Royal Society's printer, portrays the king who had held him for nearly twenty years; the 'Capital Offence' and the head he 'most probably' would have lost are his own reasoning about a native, not a recorded case. Davy and Forbes wrote as servants of the power that had ended the kingdom, and Forbes explicitly turns the rule into evidence of a king's pretence. Coomaraswamy, writing in the first decade of the twentieth century to recover the island's own craft tradition, presents the same rules as the order of a settled society. No text of the rule in the kingdom's own words was found for this film, and none of these writers quotes one.
historical_thread.how_it_binds: The C026 digest's strangest line is that stinginess, though it springs from attachment to one's own things, arises as not bearing those things to become common to others, and therefore sits with aversion and never with greed. Most places that could carry stinginess carry a hoard, and a hoard reads as greed; the digest forbids exactly that equation. Knox's rule is a hoard with the having taken out. The people could have the look: 'there is a Clay which is as white'. What they could not have was the lime, which the rule calls 'peculiar to Royal Houses and Temples', the precise opposite of the Margaya's word 'common'. So the rule gave its owners nothing visible that others lacked; its only content was that something must not become common, which is the definition. C022 sharpens the comparison: Pradeepika's third mark of stinginess is not bearing that another should have wealth like one's own, and the first of the five things it is counted by is a dwelling. And then C026 stops the film from going further than the texts. They say envy, stinginess and remorse come only sometimes, one at a time, with aversion; the rule is described from 1681 to after 1815, across seven reigns, by writers who never saw it written down. A thing that lasts a hundred and forty years is not a moment of mind, and the digest's own warning is that the scheme is not a way of reading people and a camera cannot show which factor is present. The film therefore lays the definition beside the rule and reads no one's mind, and it turns the digest's warning into its method: a camera that, by the captive's own account, could never have told the forbidden white from the permitted one. Whether the five kinds' fourth word, vaṇṇa (in Pradeepika varṇa), which can mean colour as well as beauty and praise, bears on a reserved white is a question for an expert and is not used.
what_is_certain: Knox, An Historical Relation of the Island Ceylon (1681), Part III ch. VI: the people 'are not permitted to build their houses above one story high, neither may they cover with tiles, nor whiten their walls with lime, but there is a Clay which is as white, and that they use sometimes'.

Knox, Part IV ch. III: he and his boy finished a house the villagers had begun and 'whitened the Walls with Lime, according to my own Countrey fashion. But in doing this I committed a Capital Offence: for none may white their Houses with Lime, that being peculiar to Royal Houses and Temples. But being a Stranger nothing was made of it, because I did it in ignorance: had it been a Native that had so done, it is most probable it would have cost him his Head, or at the least a great Fine.'

Knox, Part II ch. I: the king's stone pedestals were 'whitened with Lime and laid in Oyl, so that they look purely white'. Part IV ch. XIV: among the privileges allowed to white men, 'their Houses may be whitened with Lime'. Neither passage is used in the film.

Davy, An Account of the Interior of Ceylon (1821), p. 256: the chiefs' walls were covered with cow-dung plaster 'or with a wash of white clay, the use of lime for the purpose being prohibited, and appropriated solely to royal palaces and temples'; the people's houses were 'invariably thatched; only those of the highest rank being permitted to have tiled roofs'.
Davy, p. 317: among the last king's works were 'the lake of Kandy, which was made at this time' and 'many new buildings, particularly the present Pattiripooa', in a narrative placed after about 1806.

Forbes, Eleven Years in Ceylon (1840), vol. I p. 78: the king did not permit anyone 'to have a house two stories high, nor to build one with windows, nor even to roof with tiles, nor whitewash mud walls, without obtaining the royal sanction'.

Coomaraswamy, Mediaeval Sinhalese Art (1908), pp. 33–34: 'plastered walls, tiled roofs, finials and two-storied buildings were forbidden to all save the King, temples, and the highest officers'; p. 135 quotes Forbes and Davy.

D'Oyly's Sketch of the Constitution of the Kandyan Kingdom, in its 1833 Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society printing, was searched: it has no rule about lime, whitewash, house tiles or storeys. Tiles appear there only as a potters' service to the king.

The octagon and the lake are attributed to the reign of Sri Vikrama Rajasinha (1798–1815) by Davy and by current sources; the precinct stands in Kandy District (the Pattirippuwa is OSM way 217317800, 'Kandy District, Central Province').
what_is_disputed: The terms of the rule. Knox (1681) and Davy (1821), the two eyewitnesses, give a flat prohibition; Forbes (1840) says whitewashing was forbidden 'without obtaining the royal sanction'; Knox himself records that white men were allowed it, which is a royal allowance of a kind. Coomaraswamy (1908) extends the permission to 'the highest officers', where Davy says the chiefs used white clay. The versions are kept apart.

The penalty. 'Capital offence' is Knox's phrase, and the head or 'great Fine' is his supposition about what would have happened to a native. No case of anyone punished for whitewashing was found. Popular retellings that whitewashing 'was punishable by death' keep the phrase and drop the rest of the sentence.

The lake's date. Wikipedia and a Commons description give 1807; the same Wikipedia article reports 'according to D'Oyley' that the dam was built between 1810 and 1812 (D'Oyly's diary was not reached); Davy gives no year but places the lake among works under way after about 1806. Kept apart.

The octagon's date and builder. Current sources credit the royal architect Devendra Mulacharya and the last reign; a date of 1802–1803 circulates without a source found here, and Davy's narrative places 'the present Pattiripooa' in a period after about 1806. Could not be settled.

The cloud wall. Wikipedia says it was left unfinished when the kingdom fell and that its triangular openings once held lamps; neither claim was traced to a source. Its length (Wikipedia, 633.82 m) is unsourced. Nothing about it is used beyond what is on screen.
A figure impossible on its own terms: Wikipedia gives the lake an extent of 6,544 m² beside a circumference of 3.21 km; a lake with that shoreline would be many times larger. Not used.

What today's white is. Whether any of the precinct's present surfaces are lime-washed, rather than painted with modern materials, could not be confirmed. The film does not claim they are lime; it claims only that the captive said the eye could not tell.

When the rule ended. No abolition was found in any source reached. It is presumed to have lapsed with the kingdom in 1815, but that is an inference, and the voice says only that no account says when it ended.

what_to_film: The lake parapet from the far bank and from the water's edge, under even cloud: long zooms that start on pure white and end on the scalloped wall doubled in still water.
The octagon and the precinct's long white outer walls from outside the precinct and from across the lake, zooming out from white mouldings to the whole front. Exterior only; no one framed.
Close frontal texture of a plastered wall in the precinct, only where permitted and only above head height: the grain of the wash, water streaks, repairs in a slightly different white.
Ordinary houses on the slopes around the lake, zooming out from a white wall to a whole hillside of pale houses. No faces, no windows looked into, no identifiable house number or name.

The payoff: from the Arthur's Seat viewpoint on Rajapihilla Mawatha, one uninterrupted zoom from a white that fills the frame to the widest view of the basin, the precinct and the town under the same sky, held at the end.
Wild sound of the lake and the town under cloud: water, birds, distant traffic. No temple drums, chanting or loudspeakers.
suggested_location.access: The lake shore paths, the lakeside road and the Arthur's Seat viewpoint are public; the precinct's outer walls and the octagon can be seen from the esplanade and from across the lake. Tripods and long lenses near the temple sit inside a high-security zone, and permission is needed from the temple administration (the Diyawadana Nilame's office) and the police for any tripod work near the precinct, and from the Department of Archaeology and the Central Cultural Fund for the heritage property. No drone: flying near the temple is prohibited, and the treatment does not need one. Close texture shots inside the precinct need the temple's consent and must avoid all worship. The residential hillsides are private; houses are filmed only from public ground at a distance, and permission is sought for any single house that becomes the object of a long zoom. All of this is desk research and unverified.
suggested_location.best_time: A still, overcast late morning, with high bright cloud and no rain, when the lake is flat and the hills are clear. The town has rain in both monsoon seasons; the drier months are roughly January to April. Avoid the Esala festival season (usually July or August) and full-moon days, when the precinct and the lake shore are crowded and security is heaviest.

suggested_location.research_note: Desk research only, 26 September 2026, done blind to this record's previous body. Primary texts read: Knox 1681 (Project Gutenberg edition, searched for every occurrence of lime; the three passages used are Part III ch. VI, Part IV ch. III and, not used, Part II ch. I and Part IV ch. XIV); Davy 1821 (archive.org b22014640, pp. 256 and 317); Forbes 1840 (archive.org, vol. I p. 78); Coomaraswamy 1908 (archive.org, pp. 33–34 and 135); D'Oyly's Sketch in its 1833 JRAS printing (archive.org jstor-25581749), searched and found to contain none of the building rules usually credited to it. D'Oyly's diary, the Lankapradeepa and any Sinhala-language source were not reached. Coordinates are those of the Pattirippuwa (OSM way 217317800), which Nominatim places in Kandy District, Central Province; the Arthur's Seat viewpoint (OSM node 4157023134, 7.2890, 80.6399) is also in Kandy District. District budget: Kandy stood at 3 on the slate without GRP-02 and GRP-03 (IDEA-0062, IDEA-0144, IDEA-0181); the GRP-02 procession film in the same precinct (IDEA-0018) was refused and the GRP-03 mountain-pass film (IDEA-0034) was refused, so this film takes Kandy to 4, within the preferred range. Archetype: a royal precinct read through a building rule; no palace or sumptuary-law film is on the slate or in either group. The nearest neighbours are a GRP-02 museum film on the same kingdom's throne (IDEA-0014, in Colombo) and the temple-in-use films elsewhere on the slate; the temple here is only ever a white outer wall. Treatment: the proposal's hard-noon, locked 200 mm treatment was dropped because two finished films in this group already use a locked noon frame (IDEA-0039) and a locked long lens on one bearing (IDEA-0035). This film is the only one in either group lit by overcast, the only one built on the optical zoom, and one of the few with no drone; the group's other proposals are a first-sun traverse (0033), a sunset bearing (0035), a noon descent (0039), a dusk interior dolly (0043), a monsoon macro (0044, held) and a dawn-fog rack focus (0045). Persons: Robert Knox is named in the voice and in no other film's voice on the slate, in the finished GRP-02 and GRP-03 records, or in the other proposals (the refused 0018 and 0034 had planned to use him). Davy is already named in IDEA-0014's voice, so here he is 'a surgeon with the army'; Forbes and Coomaraswamy are described, not named; no king is named. Images: four Commons files confirmed through the API for existence and licence, and each thumbnail viewed; the two viewpoint photographs were taken in sun and are for composition only. Fallback in a different district: Ridi Vihara (Kurunegala), where a Kandyan-period upper temple would show a temple's privileged white in a village landscape; it is weaker, because Knox's rule is about the king's and the people's houses and the precinct is the only place where both whites share a frame, and its lower shrine is a painted cave, an archetype already used.

unknowns: Whether the royal whites and the hillside whites actually read alike on camera under cloud, and at which focal lengths; this is the payoff and must be tested on a recce.
Whether any present surface in the precinct is lime-washed.
Permissions for tripod and long-lens work at the esplanade, on the shore and at the viewpoint, and the temple administration's view of the film's subject.
Whether the long zoom needed (from roughly 1000 mm equivalent to wide) can be done in a single optical move with a broadcast lens, or must be designed around a shorter range.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location was proposed by Claude on 2026-09-26 and awaits Chathura's review; no verdict has been given. The rule is quoted from the 1681 and 1821 eyewitness accounts and from later writers as texts; everything about access, light, surfaces and permissions is desk research and unverified. No scene or shot is decided here.
